Tellez" institute: "University of California, Davis" date: today date-format: long format: revealjs: html-math-method: mathjax slide-number: true height: 900 width: 1600 code-line-numbers: true code-overflow: wrap smooth-scrawl: true theme: [simple, html/custom.scss] incremental: true title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: img/dubois-spiral-2.png data-background-size: contain data-background-position: right data-background-color: "#dc354a" --- # Plan for today {.center background-color="#dc354a"} . . . Controlling for confounds . . . Intuition . . . Limitations # Where are we so far? . . . Want to estimate the effect of X on Y . . . Elemental confounds get in our way . . . DAGs + `ggdag()` to model causal process . . . figure out **which** variables to control for and which to avoid ## Do waffles cause divorce? Remember, we have strong reason to believe the South is **confounding** the relationship between Waffle Houses and divorce rates: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: notes Speak about true effects and null effects ::: # A problem we share with Lincoln {.center background-color="#dc354a"} . . . We need to **control (for) the South** . . . It has a bad influence on divorce, waffle house locations, and the integrity of the union . . . But how do we do *control* (for) the South? And what does that even *mean*? ## We've already done it One way to adjust/control for backdoor paths is with **multiple regression**: . . . In general: $Y = \alpha + \beta_1X_1 + \beta_2X_2 + \dots$ . . . In this case: $Y = \alpha + \beta_1Waffles + \beta_2South$ . . . In multiple regression, coefficients ($\beta_i$) are different: they describe the relationship between **X1** and **Y**, *after adjusting for the X2, X3, X4, etc.* ## What does it mean to control? ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} $Y = \alpha + \beta_1Waffles + \beta_2South$ Three ways of thinking about $\color{red}{\beta_1}$ here: - The relationship between Waffles and Divorce, **controlling for the South** - The relationship between Waffles and Divorce that **cannot be explained by the South** - The relationship between Waffles and Divorce, **comparing *among* similar states (South vs. South, North vs. North)** ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](img/wooden-puzzle.jpeg){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## Comparing models Let's fit two models of the effect of GDP on life expectancy, one with controls and one without: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} no_controls = lm(lifeExp ~ gdpPercap, data = gap) controls = lm(lifeExp ~ gdpPercap + pop + year, data = gap) ``` ::: . . . Population and year might be forks here: they affect both economic activity and life expectancy . . . ::: callout-note I've re-scaled gdp (10,000s) and population (millions) ::: ## The regression table {.scrollable} We can compare models using a **regression table**; many different functions, we'll use `huxreg()` from the `huxtable` package . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} huxreg("No controls" = no_controls, "With controls" = controls) ``` ::: ::: callout-note Format: `huxreg("label for model 1" = model_1, "label for model 2" = model_2, ...)` ::: ## The regression table {.scrollable} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} huxreg("No controls" = no_controls, "With controls" = controls) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

So house size is confounding the relationship between 🚽 and 💰 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ## Controlling for size {.scrollable} What happens if we control for how large a house is? ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - The effect goes very close to zero (by house price standards), and is even negative ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} controls = lm(price ~ bathrooms + sqft_living, data = house_prices) huxreg("No controls" = no_controls, "Controls" = controls) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## Does this actually work? Back to the waffles These are examples with real data, where we can't know for sure if our controls are doing what we think . . . Only way to know for sure is with made-up data, where we **know** the effects ex ante: . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fake = tibble(south = sample(c(0, 1), size = 50, replace = TRUE), waffle = rnorm(n = 50, mean = 20, sd = 4) + 10 * south, divorce = rnorm(n = 50, mean = 20, sd = 2) + 8 * south) ``` ::: # What do we know? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fake = tibble(south = sample(c(0, 1), size = 50, replace = TRUE), waffle = rnorm(n = 50, mean = 20, sd = 4) + 10*south, divorce = rnorm(n = 50, mean = 20, sd = 2) + 8*south) ``` ::: We *know* that waffles have **0 effect** on divorce We *know* that the south has an effect of **10** on divorce We *know* that the south has an effect of **8** on waffles ## Controlling for the South Fit a **naive** model without controls, and the correct one **controlling** for the South: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} naive_waffles = lm(divorce ~ waffle, data = fake) control_waffles = lm(divorce ~ waffle + south, data = fake) ``` ::: ## The results Perfect! Naive model is **confounded**; but controlling for the South, we get pretty close to the truth (0 effect) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Naive modelControl South
(Intercept)12.586 ***20.012 ***
(2.065)   (1.651)   
waffle0.450 ***0.014    
(0.083)   (0.078)   
south        7.329 ***
        (0.921)   
nobs50        50        
*** p < 0.001; ** p < 0.01; * p < 0.05.
``` ::: ::: ## What's going on? . . . In our made-up world, if we control for the South we can get back the **uncounfounded** estimate of Divorce \~ Waffles . . . But what's `lm()` doing under-the-hood that makes this possible? ## What's going on? ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} - `lm()` is *estimating* $South \rightarrow Divorce$ and $South \rightarrow Waffles$ - it is then subtracting out or **removing** the effect of South on Divorce and Waffles - what's left is the relationship between Waffles and Divorce, *adjusting for the influence of the South on each* ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](img/controls-heiss.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## Visualizing controlling for the South This is the **confounded** relationship between waffles and divorce (zoomed out) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ## Add the south We can see what we already know: states in the South tend to have *more divorce*, and *more waffles* ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Effect of south on divorce $South \rightarrow Divorce = 10$ How much higher, on average, divorce is in the South than the North ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Remove effect of South on divorce Regression **subtracts out** the effect of the South on divorce ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Next: effect of South on waffles $South \rightarrow Waffles = 8$ How many more, on average, Waffle Houses there are in the South than the North ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ## Subtract out the effect of south on waffles Regression **subtracts out** the effect of the South on waffles ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## What's left over? The true effect of waffles on divorce $\approx$ 0 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: # The other confounds {.center background-color="#dc354a"} ## The perplexing pipe Remember, with a perplexing pipe, controlling for Z blocks the effect of X on Y: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Simulation Let's make up some data to show this: every unit of foreign aid increases corruption by 8; every unit of corruption increases the number of protest by 4 . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fake_pipe = tibble(aid = rnorm(n = 200, mean = 10), corruption = rnorm(n = 200, mean = 10) + 8 * aid, protest = rnorm(n = 200, mean = 10) + 4 * corruption) ``` ::: . . . What is the true effect of aid on protest? Tricky since the effect **runs through** corruption . . . For every unit of aid, corruption increases by 8; and for every unit of corruption, protest increases by 4... . . . The effect of aid on protest is $4 \times 8 = 32$ ## The data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} | aid| corruption| protest| |-----:|----------:|-------:| | 9.72| 85.35| 350.74| | 10.00| 89.95| 370.69| | 9.35| 83.80| 344.68| | 11.51| 102.29| 418.37| | 9.99| 89.51| 367.82| | 9.93| 89.49| 368.00| ::: ::: ## Bad controls Remember, with a **pipe** controlling for Z (corruption) is a **bad idea** . . . Let's fit two models, where one makes the mistake of controlling for corruption . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} right_model = lm(protest ~ aid, data = fake_pipe) bad_control = lm(protest ~ aid + corruption, data = fake_pipe) ``` ::: ## Bad controls Notice how the model that mistakenly controls for Z tells you that X basically has no effect on Y (*wrong*) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Correct modelBad control
(Intercept)48.127 ***9.685 ***
(3.241)   (0.887)   
aid32.167 ***-0.120    
(0.321)   (0.491)   
corruption        4.017 ***
        (0.061)   
nobs200        200        
*** p < 0.001; ** p < 0.01; * p < 0.05.
``` ::: ::: ## The exploding collider Remember, with an exploding collider, controlling for M creates strange correlations between X and Y: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Simulation Let's make up some data to show this: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fake_collider = tibble(x = rnorm(n = 100, mean = 10), y = rnorm(n = 100, mean = 10), m = rnorm(n = 100, mean = 10) + 8 * x + 4 * y) ``` ::: - X has an effect of 8 on M - Y has an effect of 4 on M - X has no effect on Y ## The data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} | x| y| m| |---------:|---------:|--------:| | 9.972584| 12.208321| 139.0415| | 10.294208| 10.958590| 136.5327| | 9.715819| 9.400894| 125.1396| | 10.680276| 11.844909| 142.3984| | 12.035113| 11.343354| 152.0356| | 9.080420| 10.709459| 125.6194| ::: ::: ## Bad controls What's the true effect of X on Y? it's zero Remember, with a **collider** controlling for M is a **bad idea** Let's fit two models, where one makes the mistake of controlling for M ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} right_model = lm(y ~ x, data = fake_collider) collided_model = lm(y ~ x + m, data = fake_collider) ``` ::: ## Bad controls Notice how the model that mistakenly controls for M tells you that X has a strong, **negative** effect on Y (*wrong*) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Correct modelCollided!
(Intercept)9.153 ***-1.803 ***
(1.031)   (0.308)   
x0.085    -1.938 ***
(0.103)   (0.047)   
m        0.240 ***
        (0.005)   
nobs100        100        
*** p < 0.001; ** p < 0.01; * p < 0.05.
``` ::: ::: ## Colliding as sample selection Most of the time when we see a collider, it's because we're looking at a weird **sample** of the population we're interested in . . . Examples: the non-relationship between height and scoring, among NBA players; the (alleged) negative correlation between how surprising and reliable findings are, among published research ## Hiring at Google Imagine Google wants to hire the best of the best, and they have two criteria: interpersonal skills, and technical skills . . . Say Google can measure how socially and technically skilled someone is (0-100) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fake_google = tibble(social_skills = rnorm(n = 200, mean = 50, sd = 10), tech_skills = rnorm(n = 200, mean = 50, sd = 10)) ``` ::: . . . The two are **causally unrelated**: one does not affect the other; improving someone's social skills would not hurt their technical skills ## The data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} | social_skills| tech_skills| |-------------:|-----------:| | 50.23| 41.04| | 32.11| 33.72| | 61.63| 71.29| | 47.74| 47.30| | 57.99| 32.59| | 42.05| 56.88| | 38.87| 41.43| | 32.54| 52.51| ::: ::: ## Simulate the hiring process Now imagine that they add up the two skills to see a person's **overall quality**: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fake_google %>% mutate(total_score = social_skills + tech_skills) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

If we only look at Google workers we see a **trade-off** between social and technical skills: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-40-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Limitations It's cool that we can control for a **confound**, or avoid colliders/pipes and get back **the truth** . . . But there are big limitations we must keep in mind when evaluating research: - We need to know what to control for (confident in our DAG) . . . - We need to have data on the controls (e.g., data on Z) . . . - We need our data to measure the variable well (e.g., \# of homicides a good proxy for crime?) ## Stuff that's hard to measure **Ability** is a likely **fork** for the effect of Education on Earnings; but how do you measure ability? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](14-dags_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-41-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## 🚨 Your turn: pipes, colliders 🚨 Using the templates in the class script: - Make a **realistic** pipe scenario - Use models to show that everything goes wrong when you *mistakenly* control for the pipe - Make a **realistic** fork scenario - Use models to show that everything goes wrong when you *fail to control* for the fork ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: :::
